analysis.one_liner: Allows Americans to import lower-cost prescription drugs from Canada and other developed countries.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to let Americans buy cheaper prescription drugs from Canada and other countries drew 31 cosponsors and two committee hearings, but was never brought to a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the government to set up a legal system for importing prescription drugs from Canada within 90 days and from countries like Australia, Japan, and those in Europe within a year. It would also let individuals order from licensed Canadian pharmacies right away, and it would make it illegal for drug companies to block imports by charging exporters more, cutting off supplies, or tweaking formulations to keep cheaper versions out of the U.S. The bill never came to a vote: it sat in the Senate health committee after two hearings and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions, especially seniors and people paying full price for brand-name drugs, who could buy the same medicines at the lower prices charged in other wealthy countries. U.S. pharmacies and wholesalers that register to import, and Canadian pharmacies that register to export, would also gain a new legal business channel.

how_it_helps.text: The bill states in its findings that Americans pay up to five times more than consumers in other countries and estimates that open drug markets could save U.S. consumers at least $38 billion a year.

It requires the Health and Human Services Secretary to write regulations allowing importation from Canada within 90 days and from Australia, EU countries, Japan, New Zealand, and Switzerland within a year.
It allows immediate personal importation of prescription drugs from licensed Canadian pharmacies, capped at a 90-day supply with a valid U.S. prescription.

It amends antitrust law to prohibit manufacturers from blocking importation by charging exporters higher prices, limiting supplies, or changing a drug's form for that purpose, and states that reselling in the U.S. a drug properly sold abroad is not patent infringement.

It builds in safety controls: registered importers and exporters, FDA facility inspections, chain-of-custody tracking, anti-counterfeit shipment markings, and recall coordination with foreign governments.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose U.S. prices — the highest in the world — would face competition from their own products sold cheaper abroad. Importers and exporters would pay registration and inspection fees capped at 1% of the value of drugs imported, a cost likely passed on in prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill excludes higher-risk products — biological drugs, controlled substances, intravenous and infused drugs — from importation, limiting the savings for patients on those treatments.
It actually tightens one rule: it repeals the existing exemption that let individuals import controlled substances for personal medical use.

The strongest good-faith objection, pressed by the FDA and the industry, was that imports from foreign pharmacies cannot be verified as reliably as the U.S. supply chain. The bill answers this with registration, inspections, tracked shipments, and recall agreements, but the system is untested and enforcement depends on regulators doing the work.
Lower effective U.S. prices would reduce brand-name manufacturers' revenue, which critics argue could mean less spent on developing new drugs.
Administering the program is not free: importers and exporters pay registration and inspection fees, capped at 1% of the value of drugs imported, to fund FDA oversight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential gain for consumers is large and the design is unusually careful for an importation bill: it channels imports through registered, inspected pharmacies and wholesalers, tracks every lot of drugs, excludes the riskiest product categories, and uses antitrust law to stop manufacturers from quietly sabotaging imports. The main honest concerns are residual safety risk in a new supply chain and reduced industry revenue for research. On balance, the bill traded a modest, regulated risk for a large, concrete price benefit to consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee, got hearings there and in the Judiciary Committee, but was never brought up for a vote, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Byron Dorgan introduced the bill on April 21, 2004, with original cosponsors including Republicans Olympia Snowe, John McCain, Trent Lott, and Lincoln Chafee alongside Democrats Ted Kennedy, Tom Daschle, and others — a deliberately bipartisan lineup.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The HELP Committee held hearings on May 20, 2004, and the Judiciary Committee held hearings on July 14, 2004.
The bill gathered 31 cosponsors — 25 Democrats, 5 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but no committee ever voted to send it to the floor, and no floor vote ever occurred.
Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: the American market stayed closed to their own cheaper foreign sales, preserving U.S. prices that the bill itself described as the highest in the world, while consumers kept paying them.

for.name: Sen. Byron Dorgan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the push to legalize prescription drug importation.

for.name: 31 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Sens. Snowe, McCain, Kennedy, Daschle, Lott, Chafee, Stabenow, Johnson, Pryor, and Feingold.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Held a hearing on May 20, 2004 but never reported the bill out of committee, keeping it from a floor vote.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee that held the second hearing, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Held a hearing on July 14, 2004 but took no further action on the bill.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Majority leadership controlling the Senate floor calendar in the 108th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate vote despite its 31 bipartisan cosponsors.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug manufacturers and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed drug importation legislation, arguing imported drugs could not be verified as safe and that cheaper imports would undercut their U.S. prices.

against.name: Bush administration
against.role: President and Department of Health and Human Services leadership
against.what_they_did: Opposed legalizing drug importation on safety grounds, removing any pressure on the Senate to act.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — 25 Democrats, 5 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but the Senate's Republican-run committees and leadership never moved the bill to a vote.

industries.note: The bill forces them to sell to registered exporters at the same prices charged domestically, bans supply cutoffs and formulation changes aimed at blocking imports, and bars patent claims against resale of drugs properly sold abroad. Their gain from the status quo — Americans paying the world's highest brand-name prices — is the public's cost.

industries.industry: Registered importers and exporters (U.S. pharmacies and wholesalers, Canadian exporters)
industries.note: The bill makes registered pharmacies, wholesalers, and exporters the exclusive legal channel for imported drugs, with priority registration for existing significant Canadian exporters. They gain a new revenue stream while accepting registration fees, inspections, and tracking rules.

industries.industry: U.S. retail pharmacies and drug wholesalers
industries.note: As registered importers, they could buy the same drugs at foreign prices and dispense them to U.S. patients, lowering their acquisition costs.
